item.title: A global stage, a missed opportunity. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The UN General Assembly offered Prime Minister Tarique Rahman an opportunity to transcend the country’s petty political factionalism and showcase Bangladesh as a nation capable of playing a leading role on the global stage.
While this opportunity arises annually, the political transformation following the 2024 uprising lent this particular session added significance for Bangladesh.
The question now arises: Did Prime Minister Tarique Rahman make the most of this opportunity? Or did he simply follow the conventional script -- extolling his own party, vilifying opponents, and delivering a bland, bureaucratic speech on geopolitical issues that carefully avoided taking a firm stand?
It became evident right at the start of the speech that the PM would not chart a new course.
Although the nation is 55 years old, he indulged in nostalgia, recalling only the speeches delivered from that very podium by his father, the late President Ziaur Rahman, and his mother, former Prime Minister Khaleda Zia.
He could also have acknowledged that Sheikh Mujibur Rahman delivered the first-ever speech in Bangla from that same platform in 1974. Doing so would not have undermined his standing as the country’s elected representative.
Yet, no matter how grand the stage, the country’s narrow political climate leaves little room for such magnanimity.
Even when standing on the global stage, Bangladeshi leaders struggle to break free from the political divisions they leave behind at home. There have been precedents for this, and this instance was no exception.
The PM blamed the past, labelled his ousted political rivals “fascists,” and presented his party’s agenda as a blueprint for development.
It was expected that he would speak of the country’s return to the path of democracy, and it was hardly surprising that he praised the February election.
However, when the domestic practice of branding the ousted Awami League as “fascist” is exported to the global stage, it effectively amounts to painting a large segment of the nation’s population as the “enemy.”
It would have signalled a new kind of politics had he spoken solely of progress rather than portraying a fractured nation by assigning blame to others.
At one point in the speech, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman stated: “By ensuring the political and economic empowerment of the people, we aim to establish a prosperous, self-reliant, and democratic welfare state -- a nation where everyone, regardless of political affiliation, religion, or race, can live securely and safely with equal rights, honour, and dignity.”
There is no doubt that these words sound appealing to everyone.
However, it would hardly be surprising if these sentiments seemed hollow when certain party activists and supporters live in fear of arrest while facing fabricated charges, languish in prison for months without trial, or, branded as “accomplices” while being subjected to attacks, handed over to the police, and jailed on false accusations.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman touched upon several significant issues in his speech, including migration, the impact of climate change, artificial intelligence, the Rohingya crisis, the volatile global situation, and the UN’s development goals.
In each instance, the government’s programs or achievements were highlighted. In some areas, particularly regarding the avoidance of geopolitical conflict, he advocated peace efforts and disarmament.
These are standard topics in UN politics; statements made by developing nations on these matters are often heard by others but usually forgotten before they even leave UN headquarters.
However, it is worth examining how the PM’s own publicity team is attempting to present his speech to the nation.
While briefing journalists in New York, Mahdi Amin, a spokesperson for the Prime Minister’s Office, described Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s address to the UN General Assembly as “historic and groundbreaking.”
Mahdi Amin stated that, through this speech, Bangladesh had “created a new history.”
What is this new history? Reading Amin’s remarks, it appears that he views the rare occurrence of three members of the same family addressing the UN as heads of government as the “historic” event.
It was not merely the family connection, however, but the glorification of the leader that appeared to be the government spokesperson’s primary focus.
“Through this speech, the world witnessed how a head of government transforms into a true statesman,” Amin said.
He reminded the nation that the PM did not confine himself to matters concerning Bangladesh alone, he also spoke about global peace and the rights of the freedom-seeking people of Palestine, and even offered counsel to the United Nations itself.
“He presented a concrete roadmap to world leaders on how the UN can play a robust role in restoring peace, prosperity, and unity across the globe,” Mahdi Amin said at a press conference.
There is no doubt that Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s speech touched upon these issues.
However, there is room for disagreement over whether these remarks were truly “historic” or “statesmanlike.”
First, heads of government from Bangladesh have always spoken about Palestinian rights when addressing the UN.
Nor is this unique to Bangladesh; leaders from most nations speak of peace and prosperity and express a desire to see the UN play a stronger and more effective role.
These are standard talking points for developing nations at international conferences.
Second, one could not merely disagree with, but vehemently dispute, the spokesperson’s claim that Prime Minister Tarique Rahman “presented a concrete roadmap to world leaders” on how the UN could play a robust role.
While Prime Minister Tarique Rahman certainly spoke eloquently about the UN’s role and what is expected of it, can those remarks truly be described as a “roadmap?”
The prime minister was correct in stating that, in the era of globalization, conflict in one part of the world can trigger unrest and economic disaster elsewhere.
He spoke of establishing bilateral or multilateral relations among disputing states based on “equality, fairness, mutual interest, and respect for dignity,” points with which few would disagree.
“Bangladesh envisions the UN as the focal point for establishing a cooperative global society that respects each other’s independence and sovereignty,” the PM said in his speech.
These are all fine sentiments. But where is the “roadmap” for the UN here? A roadmap would typically contain specific proposals and outline concrete steps.
These remarks are undoubtedly significant, particularly in the context of post-2024 Bangladesh-India relations. However, such sentiments are not new on the global stage, and all too often remain nothing more than rhetoric once the speech concludes.
Had the prime minister wished, he could have presented concrete proposals for reforming the UN Security Council or addressing the crisis in development funding.
Regarding the Rohingya crisis, instead of merely seeking international cooperation, he could have offered specific proposals grounded in reality; he could even have announced unilateral measures to reinforce Bangladesh’s commitment to the disarmament process.
The speech would have been truly “historic” or “groundbreaking” had it put forward proposals aimed at playing a leading role in resolving problems rather than simply positioning the nation as a victim.
As it stands, however, it appears that the address amounted to little more than a routine bureaucratic exercise of reading from prepared talking points.
Sabir Mustafa is the former head of BBC Bangla and is currently working as a freelance journalist and podcaster. Views expressed are the author’s own.

item.title: Nepal's hydropower ambitions face climate reality check. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Nepal’s hydropower boom has long been touted as a cornerstone of economic growth and renewable energy, but the devastating flood in August exposed its vulnerability.

The disaster triggered by a glacial mountain collapse on the China-Nepal border killed more than 1,400 people and left thousands missing — while knocking 410 megawatts (MW), or about 10 per cent of the generation capacity, out of Nepal’s power system.

More than 90pc of Nepal’s electricity comes from hydropower, but extensive damage to its river projects has prompted questions about its energy security as climate and geological risks intensify.

“Hydropower has been a major driving force in growth of the country… generating jobs and income,” Uttam Bhlon Lama, senior vice president of the Independent Power Producers’ Association (IPPAN), told AFP.

“It was bringing huge hope and future prospects to the people,” he said, adding that the country would now have to rethink its dam-building spree.

“We have to prepare… This is our new normal.”

Over the past decade, the Himalayan nation has increased hydropower output more than fourfold to about 4,120 megawatts, according to government figures, helping connect nearly all its 30 million people to the grid.

The country had previously moved to export surplus electricity to neighbouring India and Bangladesh, seeking to turn its glacier-fed rivers into a source of revenue. Authorities suspended electricity exports after the disaster.

The major destruction of hydropower infrastructure underscored the risks of that strategy in a region where glaciers are retreating, permafrost is thawing and extreme hazards are becoming harder to predict.

‘Serious lessons’

Nepal’s energy sector accounted for about half of the infrastructure damage from the disaster, according to government assessments.

Seven hydropower projects were directly hit while generation was halted at others, removing 410 MW from the national grid.

Six hydropower projects under construction, with a combined capacity of 508 MW, were also damaged.

Rescuers have continued searching hydropower tunnels for hundreds of missing workers, engineers and other personnel, weeks after the disaster.

The scale of the damage has prompted calls for a rethink of how projects are designed and built.

The disaster has “taught us serious lessons for the future”, Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha told parliament on Wednesday.

“We must not only take stock of the damage but also learn from it and develop systems to reduce future risks,” he said.

The World Bank warned that Nepal needs to build a hydropower system capable of anticipating, absorbing and recovering from increasingly complex Himalayan hazards.

Scientists say the August disaster was caused by a complex chain of geological and climatic factors rather than a single extreme weather event.

According to the World Weather Attribution group, the massive rock-and-ice collapse was shaped by long-term warming, glacier retreat and geological instability.

‘Existential threat’

Much of Nepal’s hydropower infrastructure lies along steep river valleys fed by glaciers — terrain exposed to floods, landslides and cascading geological hazards.

“Powerhouses need to be moved higher up from the riverbeds to protect them against floods, we need better evacuation plans and stocked safehouses,” IPPAN’s Lama said.

“We should explore remotely operated systems so people are not stuck inside in case anything happens.”

The flooding has also renewed calls for diversifying the power mix in Nepal, which lacks coal or gas-fired generation capacity.

“Nepal’s electricity system, currently strained and heavily dependent on hydropower, could be made more robust through well-planned additions of solar electricity,” Germany’s development agency GIZ said in a 2024 report.

The challenge extends beyond Nepal.

Glaciers in the wider Himalayan and Hindu Kush ranges are a crucial water source for around 240 million people in the mountainous regions, as well as for another 1.65 billion people in the South Asian and Southeast Asian river valleys below.

Basanta Raj Adhikari, director at the Centre for Disaster Studies at Tribhuvan University, said the Himalayas must be monitored regionally for hotspots to develop early warning systems.

“I call it the fate of the Himalayan people,” he told AFP.

“It can happen anywhere in the world but the Himalayas are experiencing adverse impacts due to climate change and anthropogenic activity,” he said.

“We have to design climate-resilient infrastructures. That is our top priority because we are (facing) existential threat.”

item.title: The relationship between progress and cancer. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
That we're all at risk of dying from cancer is a good thing. No, really, I insist that this is true.
For what it is really saying is that we're all living long enough to die of cancer.
We're not, instead, dying young of infectious diseases, starvation, and war.
OK, fair enough, that's of small comfort to someone who has just received a cancer diagnosis. It's grossly unfair to those few who get struck down young.
From personal experience, a friend died of brain cancer at 16 years of age. My father, when announcing his own diagnosis at age 85, emailed us all to say: “I have lived long enough to get prostate cancer.”
Cancer is, barring those youthful tragedies, a disease of age and a life largely already lived. This may or may not be a comfort, but it's definitely a change.
This is the thing we need to keep in mind when we discuss things like the World Cancer Congress .
Yes, it is absolutely true that more of us die now of -- or even more of us will die of -- cancer than ever used to happen in the past.
But that's because in the past, most of us would already be dead.
We see some of the toll of those infectious diseases in the reports of the measles outbreak that has been occurring in Bangladesh. Hundreds dead. That's hundreds of individual tragedies. But it's worth reminding ourselves what it was like not so long ago.
Even in the richest countries two and three centuries back, it was expected that half of all children would die before puberty. About half of those -- so a quarter of all babies -- in that first and most delicate year of life. Then another half -- another quarter of all children -- from accidents and infections.
We would assume that a grieving parent today would have been most unlucky. Back then it was normal for this to happen several times in each family.
Once through those childhood diseases, lifespans were not too far off our own. Someone who reached 20 years of age could well expect to reach 60, for example. Probably the most dangerous thing was childbirth for women. Or war, of course.
What changed things was, in order, drains and drinkable water, followed by better nutrition, and only after that, the antibiotics and vaccines that deal with the infectious diseases themselves.
This is still ongoing, new vaccines arrive all the time. The HPV one has been around a bit more than a decade and already in the UK, cervical cancer among the under-30s has fallen to an effective zero.
It's possible to have great hope for the ongoing trials of mRNA vaccines -- the original intention was always for anti-cancer treatments. Covid was just a happenstance.
But the thing to grasp about high cancer rates in modern populations is that this isn't a result of modern life poisoning us and it's not even, despite what some will claim, because of our diet or exercise regimes. It's because, by any historical standard, we're rich these days.
You know that saying that the rich also have their problems? This is one of them, living long enough to get cancer.
We'd still like to beat cancer, sure we would. But that this is the problem we're worrying about now is evidence of how far we've already come.
Tim Worstall is a senior fellow at the Adam Smith Institute in London.

item.title: Bridging the last mile. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Two contrasting stories published in these pages highlight the starkly uneven reality of rural development in Bangladesh.
In Khulna’s Dakope upazila , the completion of the 661-metre Bhadra Bridge has finally connected seven isolated unions, ending decades of precarious ferry dependence for about 350,000 residents.
Meanwhile, in Tangail’s Bhuapur upazila , 10,000 citizens across seven villages along the Louhajang River still rely on a single, risky boat, waiting for a basic bridge that, 50 years later, is yet to be built.
These two narratives illustrate, above all else, a persistent flaw in our national planning.
While high-profile megaprojects absorb political capital and public attention, true equitable growth must be measured by last-mile connectivity.
A simple river crossing fundamentally transforms rural life: It allows, among others, children to reach schools safely, ensures critically ill patients access emergency healthcare without delay, and provides farmers direct access to bigger markets.
For marginalized communities, the lack of basic infrastructure is nothing if not a systemic failure that deprives them of fundamental socio-economic opportunities.
With that said, we must also contend with the sobering, familiar issue of exceeding costs and timelines for our infrastructure projects.
Originally tendered in 2016 for Tk 37.43 crore with a targeted completion date of early 2018, the Bhadra Bridge suffered multiple contractor defaults, administrative delays, and repeated timeline extensions. That the project ultimately dragged on for eight years and cost Tk 50.75 crore reflects an administration that is incompetent and unable to meet deadlines and budgets.
This culture of routine delay, fiscal inflation, and lax procurement oversight has plagued our public works sector for far too long. Inflated budgets and missed deadlines waste taxpayer money and delay vital public services, and we must have better discipline as a nation. That is non-negotiable.
Delivering infrastructure to the last mile is essential, but doing so on time and strictly within budget must become the standard for public governance.

item.title: A disgraceful assault. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The attack on the Radda MCH-FP Centre in Mirpur must be called out for what it was: A despicable act that sinks to the absolute lowest depths of moral bankruptcy.
Under the cover of darkness, a mob of over 200 masked men armed with hammers, sticks, and heavy excavators bound and gagged security guards before attempting to raze the healthcare facility to the ground.
That they looted essential medical equipment, ultrasound machinery, and cash from a centre that provided services primarily to disadvantaged and low-income people shows that, beyond being an illegal land grab, this was a barbaric, gutless act of aggression and brings profound national shame upon us all.
For five decades, the centre has served as a sanctuary for low-income families, providing essential care to over 400 underprivileged mothers, infants, and elderly patients every single day. To reduce such a vital community lifeline to a pile of rubble over a 10-katha real estate dispute is a heinous crime.
That perpetrators felt empowered to deploy heavy machinery in the heart of the capital at midnight reveals the magnitude of the impunity enjoyed by such criminals, making a mockery of law and order.
It goes without saying that this outrage demands an unyielding, zero-tolerance response. Excuses, bureaucratic delays, and political finger-pointing are completely unacceptable.
Every individual involved -- from the masked goons who wielded the hammers to those orchestrating the land grab under the guise of local associations -- must be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.
Failure to swiftly apprehend and try those responsible would signal a complete collapse of governance and a further invitation to mob rule. We expect the authorities concerned to demonstrate, through actions, that those who resort to such brutality will face uncompromising justice. Anything less is a betrayal.

item.title: Inflation seen slowing to 10.75pc in September. [ dawn ]
item.description:
KARACHI: Some stakeholders and analysts expect inflation in September to slow despite the high uncertainty caused by the ongoing Gulf war.

The financial sector expects oil prices to remain between $90 and $100 per barrel during the remaining days of September and in October.

However, the situation has once again changed after US President Donald Trump announced on Saturday that he had rejected Iran’s proposal for the Gulf war. Iran is now anticipating possible attacks from the US, raising concerns that oil prices could surge.

Analysts expect oil prices to remain around $100 per barrel if the war resumes. However, much will depend on the availability of oil supplies in the international market. Pakistan imports 70pc of its oil and gas requirements, making inflation highly sensitive to oil prices.

Stakeholders believe oil prices to hover around $100 per barrel

Pakistan’s official headline inflation rose sharply to 11.1pc year-on-year in August 2026, up from 9.2pc in July 2026.

According to a Topline Securities report, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) for September is expected to rise 10.25-10.75pc year-on-year, down from 11.1pc in August. This projection is slightly lower than the August figure, but does not represent a significant decline.

Petroleum prices have been rising daily in Pakistan and have now reached the highest level in the region. India increased petrol prices by 10pc, while Bangladesh reportedly jacked up by 16pc and Pakistan by over 50pc.

“It is not easy to assess the exact inflation figure for September as oil prices have been changing both internationally and locally. We can only expect slightly lower inflation, with a fear that it may remain close to last month’s level,” said S.S. Iqbal, a money market expert.

With inflation expected to remain at 10.25-10.75pc in September 2026, real interest rates are likely to stand at 75-125 basis points, lower than Pakistan’s historical average of 200-300 basis points, according to the Topline report.

Electricity, housing, food and construction costs have also witnessed increases, suggesting that inflation could come in above analysts’ expectations, particularly if the Gulf war continues for an extended period.

At the same time, Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia are preparing to respond to a possible new conflict involving the Houthis and the kingdom, adding to uncertainty over oil prices and supplies. Any disruption could have a direct impact on Pakistan’s economy and inflation.

Pakistan’s foreign exchange reserves, currently exceeding $21.4 billion, may provide some cushion against higher oil import costs. However, they cannot prevent inflationary pressures from rising if the conflict continues and international energy prices remain elevated.

Published in Dawn, September 27th, 2026

item.title: Five days inside the contradictions of the United Nations. [ dawn ]
item.description:
UNITED NATIONS: Only at the United Nations can a journalist walk through a corridor and suddenly find himself face to face with a prime minister, pause before a sculpture symbolising peace, read the words of a Persian poet written on a wall, and then rush outside to report on a protest against a war thousands of miles away.

For five days, I lived inside that extraordinary contradiction while covering the high-level debate of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York. The official high-level week brought heads of state and government from around the world to the UN headquarters between September 22 and 26.

The first thing one begins to notice at the United Nations is the art.

There are sculptures, statues and works donated by countries that seem to confront you at every turn. They are reminders of peace, humanity, war and the hope that nations can somehow learn to live together.

Even before you enter the United Nations, the place begins to tell its story.

As you approach the Secretariat Building, you encounter Barbara Hepworth’s Single Form, the large abstract bronze standing beside the circular pool. Donated by Jacob Blaustein, it rises quietly against the building, its simple, powerful shape inviting a visitor to pause before entering a place where the world’s conflicts are debated.

Nearby stands St. George Slaying the Dragon, a sculpture presented to the United Nations by the Soviet Union. The familiar image of St. George defeating the dragon takes on a different meaning here, surrounded by the flags and institutions of an organisation created in the aftermath of war.

And then there is Antun Augustinčić’s Peace Monument, the mounted figure holding a sword and an olive branch. The Yugoslav/Croatian sculptor had wanted its silhouette to be visible from the East River, so that the idea of peace could announce itself even before a visitor reached the building.

Further along is Carl Fredrik Reuterswärd’s Non-Violence, the bronze revolver with its barrel tied into a knot, a gift from Luxembourg. Nearby, Evgeniy Vuchetich’s Let Us Beat Swords into Ploughshares shows a man transforming a sword into a tool for cultivating the earth.

Taken together, these sculptures seem to form a kind of preface to the United Nations: the human figure, the struggle against violence, the rejection of weapons and the hope that instruments of destruction can be transformed into instruments of peace.

And then you enter the building, where the symbols continue. On an entrance are the words of the great Persian poet Saadi, reminding us that human beings are parts of one body, created from the same essence — and that when one part suffers, the others cannot remain at peace.

And then, inside the building, you encounter the words of Saadi, the great Persian poet, written on a wall.

His famous lines describe human beings as parts of one body, created from the same essence. When one part suffers, the others cannot remain at peace.

I kept returning to those words during these five days.

Because almost everywhere I looked, I saw the world struggling with the very idea they express.

Iran and the United States were at the centre of intense diplomatic activity. Gaza dominated conversations inside the building and protests outside it. The war in Ukraine continued to draw attention, while India and Pakistan brought their familiar confrontation to the international forum.

The United Nations seemed to contain the whole contradiction of our age: an institution built on the idea that humanity can act together, confronted every day by evidence of how difficult that remains.

Outside the gates, protesters gathered in large numbers as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu arrived to address the UN General Assembly. Inside, delegations walked out during his speech.

And there I was, moving between the demonstrations, the diplomatic meetings, the press conferences and the Assembly hall, doing what journalists do — watching, listening, asking questions and trying to understand what was happening behind the carefully prepared language of diplomacy.

At one point, I actually bumped into Netanyahu.

It was not a planned interview or a formal meeting. It was simply one of those extraordinary moments possible only at the United Nations, where presidents, prime ministers, diplomats, security officers, journalists and interpreters are constantly crossing one another’s paths.

The security arrangements themselves became part of the story.

During the US president’s stay in New York, security around the United Nations was extraordinarily tight. Motorcades moved through sealed streets, access was restricted and every movement of a major leader seemed choreographed. The arrival of leaders such as the Syrian and Turkish presidents added to the atmosphere.

Then the intensity would ease.

A major leader would leave, the barricades would move, the corridors would become less crowded, and suddenly the United Nations would feel almost ordinary again—until another motorcade arrived.

That rhythm is something a television broadcast cannot quite capture.

At the UN, diplomacy is not only what leaders say from the podium. It is also the waiting, the corridors, the security checks, the hurried whispers, the chance encounters and the small conversations between meetings.

Pakistan’s diplomatic role was another important part of my coverage.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the Assembly as Islamabad continued efforts to facilitate dialogue between Iran and the United States. Shehbaz later said Pezeshkian regarded the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding as fully acceptable to Iran and was prepared to move it forward.

That is the other side of covering the UN.

You see confrontation, but you also see countries trying to create channels through which confrontation might be reduced.

And sometimes the most memorable moments have nothing to do with the major powers.

Only at the United Nations could I find myself in a photograph with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman of Bangladesh, Prime Minister Lord Fakafanua of Tonga and Deputy Prime Minister Mulipola Anarosa Ale Molioo of Samoa.

Three leaders from three very different parts of the world, standing together in New York.

Only at the United Nations.

The photograph captures something that statistics cannot. The General Assembly has 193 member states, each represented with one vote. Yet the world represented inside that building is vastly more complicated than a list of countries and votes.

Every delegation carries its own history. Every leader brings his country’s anxieties. Every journalist arrives carrying questions.

And outside, the protesters carry their anger.

For five days, I walked past the sculptures and statues, past the flags and security barriers, past presidents and prime ministers, past demonstrations and diplomatic receptions.

And each time I saw Saadi’s words on the wall, they seemed to ask the same simple question:

If we really are parts of one body, how can one part suffer while the rest remains at peace?

The United Nations has no easy answer. Perhaps that is why the question is still written on its wall.

And perhaps that is why, after five days of covering the world’s most powerful people, the image I carry with me is not of a speech or a motorcade.

It is of people from Bangladesh, Tonga, Samoa and Pakistan standing together for a photograph.

Only at the United Nations.

When will Bangla take its place at the UN?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
There are moments in a nation's history when a language becomes much more than a means of communication. It becomes a symbol of identity, dignity, and collective struggle. For Bangladesh, Bangla is precisely such a language.
The blood shed during the Language Movement of 1952 transformed the demand for linguistic rights into one of the defining chapters of the nation's history. More than seven decades later, the question is no longer whether Bangla has a place in the global linguistic landscape. It is whether that place can now be reflected in the world's foremost multilateral institution -- the United Nations.
The United Nations began its journey in 1945 with five official languages: English, French, Russian, Spanish, and Mandarin (Chinese). Arabic was added in 1973, bringing the total number of official UN languages to six. Initially, only English and French were used as the working languages of the Security Council from 1946. Russian and Spanish were added in 1969, while Mandarin was adopted for that purpose in 1974. Although Arabic became an official UN language in 1973, its use in the Security Council began only in 1982.
Spanish is the official language of 20 countries worldwide, most of which are located in Latin America -- specifically Central America, the Caribbean, and South America. However, although Spanish is widely spoken in the United States, it is not the country's federal official language.
The history of these languages offers an important perspective on the question of Bangla. Russian and Spanish waited 23 years after the establishment of the United Nations before becoming Security Council languages, while Mandarin waited 29 years. Arabic, by contrast, was adopted as a Security Council language nine years after becoming an official UN language.
The official languages of all five permanent members of the Security Council (USA, UK, France, Russia, China) are also UN languages. At the same time, no Arab country or Muslim-majority member of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) has yet secured a permanent seat on the Security Council.
Although Bangla ranks sixth worldwide in terms of the number of speakers, it enjoys official-language status in only a limited number of jurisdictions. Russian, ranking eighth, has attained official UN language status, bypassing Bangla (ranked sixth) and Portuguese (ranked seventh).
Historically, imperial powers extended the influence of their languages in tandem with the expansion of their empires. Today, four European languages are among the official languages of the United Nations, while English serves as the official language of both the United Kingdom and the United States. Arabic, meanwhile, holds official status in numerous countries across Africa and the Middle East. Against this historical and geopolitical backdrop, the inclusion of another major Asian language remains an unresolved issue.
Bangladesh's heads of state or heads of government deliver speeches in Bangla at the United Nations General Assembly every year. Bangla's international profile received a major boost in 1999, when UNESCO proclaimed February 21 International Mother Language Day. What began as a commemoration of the language martyrs of Bangladesh has since become a global observance of linguistic diversity and the right to speak one's mother tongue.
The recognition gave Bangladesh a unique opportunity to place Bangla within a broader international discourse on language, culture, and identity. Yet international recognition and institutional recognition are not the same thing.
The price of recognition
One of the most frequently cited obstacles to making Bangla an official UN language is cost. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has previously indicated that Bangladesh would need to commit at least $60 million annually to meet the additional expenses, particularly for translation and interpretation within the UN system.
By comparison, Bangladesh currently contributes approximately $300,000 a year to the UN budget, or around 0.1% of the total.
The financial challenge is therefore substantial. But technology may have changed the nature of that challenge. Artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed machine translation at a speed that would have been difficult to imagine even a decade ago.
The UN's enormous volume of documents, reports, statements, and communications requires translation between its six official languages. Extending such services to Bangla would undoubtedly require considerable investment, technical safeguards, and human oversight.
But the development of AI-assisted translation systems could potentially reduce the recurring cost substantially. Instead of viewing the $60 million figure as an unavoidable permanent expenditure, Bangladesh could explore whether an initial investment in research, development, language datasets, and AI-powered translation infrastructure could create a more sustainable model.
Such a system would still require professional translators and institutional quality control, particularly for diplomatic, legal, and technical documents. But technology could make the financial equation considerably more manageable.
This is where Bangladesh's growing information technology sector could become strategically important. The issue, therefore, should not be framed solely as a question of how much Bangladesh would have to pay. It should also be framed as a question of how Bangladesh can use its technological capabilities to reduce the cost of linguistic inclusion.
A language of more than 350 million people
The demographic case for Bangla is substantial. More than 350 million people around the world speak Bangla, placing it among the world's major languages. Yet the number of speakers alone does not determine whether a language becomes an official UN language.
Hindi, for example, has hundreds of millions of speakers but is not an official UN language. Russian, despite having considerably fewer speakers, already enjoys official status.
India's linguistic structure also makes a direct comparison between Hindi and Bangla more complicated. India has no single national language. The Constitution recognizes 22 languages, while individual states have their own official languages and English continues to play a major role in administration, higher education, and interstate communication.
Of course, international linguistic influence depends on much more than population. Political reach, economic relevance, geographic distribution, cultural influence, diplomatic utility, and institutional capacity all matter. That is why the question of Bangla's future at the UN cannot be reduced to a simple calculation of how many people speak it.
Bangla beyond Bangladesh
Bangla's geographical reach is far greater than Bangladesh alone. In addition to being the principal language of Bangladesh, Bangla is widely spoken in India, particularly in West Bengal, Tripura and Assam, as well as in other parts of eastern India.
Bangla-speaking communities also exist in Nepal, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, and Myanmar. Large Bangladeshi and Bangla-speaking communities have emerged across the Middle East, particularly in the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, and Qatar.
Beyond Asia and the Middle East, Bangla is spoken by substantial communities in the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, Germany, Australia, and Japan. This global diaspora represents an important but underutilized resource for the internationalisation of Bangla.
For millions of expatriate Bengalis, Bangla remains the language of family, culture, and community. Over the past 25 years, Bangladeshi expatriate organizations in different cities around the world have submitted memoranda to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Cultural Affairs, Bangladesh's diplomatic missions, and the United Nations, calling for Bangla to be recognized as an official UN language.
What appears to be missing is a sustained, coordinated international campaign bringing these individual efforts together under a clearly defined national strategy.
Portuguese presents another useful comparison. With a global population of speakers broadly comparable to Bengali, Portuguese is used across at least 12 countries, including Portugal and Brazil, and has an established presence alongside Spanish across Europe, Latin America, and other parts of the world.
Malay is another language with a substantial regional footprint. It is spoken in Malaysia, Indonesia, Singapore, Brunei, Timor-Leste, and parts of Thailand.
Arabic offers perhaps the most relevant precedent. It became an official UN language after the Arab states concerned agreed to shoulder the full cost of translating UN documents into Arabic.
Its recognition was therefore supported not simply by the number of speakers but by a coordinated political commitment among a group of states.
That precedent carries a clear lesson for Bangladesh: International linguistic recognition requires diplomacy, institutional preparedness, and financial commitment in addition to a large speaker population.
The global importance of a language can also be measured through economic and geopolitical influence. Approximately 1.5 billion people worldwide speak English, followed by Mandarin with around 1.1 billion, Hindi with approximately 600 million, Spanish with about 550 million, Arabic with around 370 million, Bengali with approximately 350 million, French with around 270 million, and Russian around 250 million.
But when language is assessed through economic and geopolitical power, the ranking changes. The World Economic Forum's "Power Language Index" places English, Mandarin, French, Spanish, Arabic, Russian, German, Japanese, Portuguese, and Hindi among the world's most influential languages.
The index considers factors such as economic opportunity, access to knowledge and media, geographic diplomacy, travel, and the ability to facilitate dialogue. Bangla's challenge, therefore, is not a lack of speakers. It is the comparatively limited economic and institutional power associated with the language outside its traditional geographic base. That is something Bangladesh can change.
Bangla has already acquired an extraordinary cultural legacy. Rabindranath Tagore became the first Asian Nobel laureate, receiving the Nobel Prize in Literature. Amartya Sen received the Nobel Prize in Economics, while Dr Muhammad Yunus received the Nobel Peace Prize. Bengali literature, music, cinema, and scholarship have continued to attract international audiences.
Bangla-language media have also expanded beyond Bangladesh and India. Bangla programs have been broadcast through radio and television in countries including the United States, the United Kingdom, Russia, Germany, China, Japan, the Philippines, Iran, and Pakistan. Bengali newspapers and online media platforms are published across the world, while the use of Bangla on the internet has grown significantly.
UN Radio launched Bangla-language programming in 2012, although the service was suspended in 2021 amid budget constraints during the Covid-19 pandemic. The UNDP has also published its annual report on Asia in Bangla alongside the English edition.
Meanwhile, Bangladesh's diplomatic community has been using language as a form of cultural diplomacy. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs organizes events in Dhaka to mark International Mother Language Day, with representatives of foreign missions participating. Diplomats posted in Bangladesh pay tribute to the language martyrs by laying flowers at a temporary Shaheed Minar at the Foreign Service Academy.
Some foreign diplomats posted in Dhaka have also taken up learning Bangla. These developments demonstrate that the internationalization of Bangla is already taking place, albeit incrementally and without a sufficiently coordinated strategy.
For Bangla to become an official language of the United Nations, Bangladesh would need to formally place the issue before the General Assembly and seek support for a resolution.
Such an initiative would require extensive diplomatic engagement with other member states. But diplomacy should not begin with the resolution. It should begin much earlier. It is worth noting that Bangladesh is presiding over the current session of the United Nations General Assembly.
Bangladesh would first need to build a broad coalition of countries and international organizations willing to support the initiative. It would need to demonstrate that the financial and technological requirements of incorporating Bangla into the UN system can be met.
It would also need to establish a credible institutional mechanism for translation, interpretation, terminology development, and quality control. Most importantly, the government would need to treat the issue as a long-term state policy rather than an occasional diplomatic initiative.
There is no simple population-based formula for determining which languages become official UN languages. The existing six official languages themselves demonstrate that geopolitical history, diplomatic influence, and international utility have played a major role.
Bangla is one of South Asia's major languages. Its history is inseparable from one of the world's most significant struggles for linguistic rights. Its literature has produced globally recognized figures. Its speakers span continents. Its digital presence is expanding. And its symbolic importance has already been acknowledged by the international community through International Mother Language Day.
Bangla has a history worthy of international recognition. But the question is whether Bangladesh can convert that historical and cultural capital into sustained diplomatic, technological, and economic influence.
Recognition at the United Nations would undoubtedly carry symbolic importance. It could enhance the international visibility of Bangla, strengthen Bangladesh's cultural identity, and make communication between Bengali speakers and international institutions easier.
But official recognition alone would not guarantee the global expansion of a language. Languages thrive when people have reasons to learn and use them.
That means Bangladesh must simultaneously increase the economic, technological, and cultural value of Bangla. Electronic and digital media can play a major role. Bengali cinema, drama, music, literature, publishing, educational content, software, and AI applications can all contribute to expanding the language's global reach.
The commercialization of Bangla should not be seen as a threat to its cultural identity. Rather, economic utility can reinforce cultural influence. A language that becomes useful in education, technology, entertainment, business, and international communication is more likely to cross borders and attract new learners. This is perhaps the most important lesson for Bangladesh.
The struggle for Bangla began with a demand for linguistic dignity. It evolved into a defining element of national identity.
The next stage requires a different kind of movement -- one built not only on emotion and historical memory, but also on diplomacy, technology, investment, cultural production, and economic opportunity.
Seventy years after Bangla became the state language of Pakistan's eastern wing and more than seven decades after the Language Movement, Bangladesh has an opportunity to take the language's global journey to another level.
Making Bangla an official language of the United Nations may be a long and difficult process. It may require years of diplomacy, substantial investment, and considerable institutional preparation. But the ambition itself is neither unrealistic nor misplaced.
If Bangladesh wants Bangla to speak more prominently on the world stage, it must first give the language the economic, technological, and diplomatic strength to be heard. The time has come to move from commemorating the language to strategically investing in its future.
Salahuddin Ahmaad Bablu is a senior journalist.

item.title: AI didn't give me sight. It gave me independence. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
A few months ago, I received a phone call from a mother who is blind. She was not calling to discuss technology. She was calling because she was worried about her two-year-old son.
"My son has learned that I cannot see," she told me. "He has also learned that if he stays completely quiet, I cannot find him. Sometimes he hides in a corner of the room without making a sound. Those are the moments that frighten me the most."
As she spoke, I could hear something that every parent understands: Fear for a child's safety. But for her, that fear was magnified by the simple reality that she could not rely on vision.
I suggested she try an AI-powered visual assistance app. Using the smartphone's camera, the app analyzes the surroundings and describes them aloud in real time.
A few weeks later, she called me again.
This time, her voice sounded different.
"My phone tells me, 'Your child is standing near the door.' It says, 'Your child is playing with a toy.' Sometimes it even tells me what he is holding. I can find him almost immediately."
The technology had not restored her eyesight.
But it had restored something equally important: Confidence.
That conversation stayed with me because it perfectly captured what artificial intelligence really means for many persons with disabilities.
Public discussions about AI usually focus on automation, productivity, investment, or whether machines will replace human jobs. Those conversations are important. Yet they often overlook another reality.
For millions of people with disabilities, AI is not about replacing people. It is about reducing dependence.
I know this because I live it every day.
I am a person with a visual disability, and for much of my life, ordinary tasks depended on someone else's availability.
If someone handed me a printed document, I had to ask them to read it.
If I received a business card, I had to ask whose name was written on it.
If I wanted to identify the label on a medicine bottle or read information on product packaging, I often needed another person's help.
There is nothing wrong with asking for support. We all depend on one another in different ways.
But when every simple task requires assistance, independence slowly slips away.
Artificial intelligence is changing that.
Today, I begin my mornings by reading the news independently. AI reads newspapers and online articles aloud, allowing me to follow national affairs, global events, and public debates without waiting for someone else to read them to me.
When I prepare for work, AI helps identify the colour of my clothes and suggests matching combinations.
To many people, choosing a shirt may seem insignificant.
To me, choosing my own clothes without asking another person is dignity in action.
Even this article has been shaped with the help of AI.
I speak, AI converts my words into text, and I refine the ideas. What once took hours can now be accomplished far more efficiently, allowing me to spend less time overcoming barriers and more time contributing my expertise.
Across the world, similar stories are unfolding every day.
Students are accessing textbooks more independently.
Professionals are reviewing documents and writing reports.
Entrepreneurs are managing businesses.
People are navigating unfamiliar places with greater confidence.
Families are communicating more effectively.
AI is quietly removing barriers that many people never realized existed.
However, technology alone is not enough. AI can only be transformative when the digital world itself is accessible.
An intelligent assistant cannot fully compensate for a website that cannot be navigated with a screen reader, an online form that is inaccessible from the keyboard, or a mobile application that ignores basic accessibility standards.
Accessibility remains the foundation. AI is an accelerator -- not a substitute -- for inclusive design.
As someone who has spent more than two decades working on digital accessibility, I see AI as one of the greatest opportunities to build a more inclusive society. But that opportunity will only be realized if governments, businesses, educators, developers, and technology companies intentionally include persons with disabilities in designing and testing digital products.
The disability community has long embraced the principle: "Nothing about us without us."
The same principle must guide the future of AI.
When people with disabilities participate in designing technology, AI becomes more accurate, more useful, and ultimately more human.
People sometimes ask me whether AI has changed my life.
My answer is simple.
AI did not give me sight. It gave me something I value just as much.
The freedom to read independently.
The confidence to make my own choices.
The dignity to participate more equally in society.
And for millions of people with disabilities around the world, that may be AI's most remarkable achievement.
Vashkar Bhattacharjee is a digital accessibility expert and disability rights advocate with a visual disability and over 20 years of experience. Email: vashkarbd@gmail.com .

item.title: The case for digital banks. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh Bank’s initial approval for five digital banks is an encouraging development for the country’s financial sector -- a move that can help accelerate the transition towards a more accessible, technology-driven banking system while creating new opportunities for people who remain underserved by conventional banking channels.
The proposed institutions, backed by businesses including bKash, Robi, Banglalink, and Square Group, will operate without conventional branches, providing banking services primarily through digital platforms.
This model could make financial services more convenient, particularly for people and small businesses that face difficulties accessing traditional banking facilities.
Bangladesh has already experienced rapid growth in mobile financial services, making the expansion of digital banking a natural next step.
There is also considerable potential for digital banks to support smaller borrowers and entrepreneurs: According to Bangladesh Bank, the new institutions are expected to focus on underserved customers and smaller loans rather than large-scale lending.
If managed responsibly, this could help broaden access to formal finance and support economic participation among people who have traditionally remained outside the banking system.
At the same time, innovation must be accompanied by strong safeguards. Digital banking will involve the collection and management of significant amounts of financial and personal data, making cybersecurity, consumer protection, and reliable digital infrastructure essential.
Bangladesh Bank must maintain rigorous oversight to ensure that technological convenience does not come at the expense of financial security or public confidence.
It is also important to remember that an initial approval is not a final license. The proposed banks must establish the necessary infrastructure and fulfil regulatory requirements before they can begin operations. This measured approach is welcome.
If the new banks combine innovation with accountability, security, and responsible lending, they could help make Bangladesh’s financial system more inclusive and efficient.
The move, therefore, represents a potentially important step towards a banking sector that better reflects the country’s increasingly digital economy.

item.title: Putting Bangladesh first. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s address to the 81st United Nations General Assembly was a historic moment for the nation, and we commend how he presented a broad vision for our future.
The speech outlined the values the government says should guide the country’s next chapter: Democracy, equality, accountability, dignity, opportunity, peace, and inclusive development.
The emphasis on rebuilding democratic institutions and ensuring equal rights is particularly significant -- aspiring for a nation where people, regardless of political affiliation, religion, or race, can live safely and with dignity, and where democracy extends across the country.
The focus on young people, women, and children reflects another important part of this vision.
Developing skills, creating employment, encouraging entrepreneurship, expanding women’s education and economic participation, and strengthening education, health and sports could help Bangladesh make better use of its demographic dividend.
If pursued effectively, such priorities could create a society where citizens have greater opportunities to build secure and productive lives.
The speech also placed Bangladesh within a wider global framework: Its calls for peaceful conflict resolution, multilateral cooperation, climate justice, technology transfer, and fair access to artificial intelligence demonstrate an emphasis on cooperation and shared responsibility.
Ultimately, however, the significance of this vision will depend on how firmly these principles take root at home.
Economic inclusion must reach those who have traditionally been left behind. Education and employment opportunities must translate into better prospects for young people, while women and children must be able to benefit from the country’s progress.
The speech has therefore set out an expansive vision of a safer, more democratic, inclusive and self-reliant Bangladesh.
The opportunity now lies in turning that vision into sustained action. If the values outlined at the UN become the foundation of governance and development, they could help shape a future in which progress is measured not only by economic growth, but by how widely security, dignity, and opportunity are shared.

item.title: Who gets to be Italian? The rise and rise of Islamophobia in Italy. [ middleeasteye ]
item.description:
Who gets to be Italian? The rise and rise of Islamophobia in Italy

Submitted by Dalia Ismail on Fri, 09/25/2026 - 13:30
Giorgia Meloni's announcement of a ban on the burqa and niqab in schools comes as the Italian right competes over the demonisation of Muslims
A Muslim takes part in a mass in Santa Maria in Trastevere church in Rome on 31 July 2016 (AFP)
Off

When Giorgia Meloni addressed hundreds of young supporters of her Brothers of Italy party in Rome on Sunday, she chose the school as a way of illustrating who she thought was and was not Italian. 

“It cannot be that, in an Italian classroom, Italian children are the ones who feel cornered because they have become the minority. It cannot happen,” the prime minister told Fenix, the annual festival organised by National Youth, Brothers of Italy’s youth wing. 

On Wednesday, Meloni’s government approved a ban on the burqa and niqab in schools and announced that a 30 percent cap will be imposed on children without Italian citizenship or poor knowledge of the Italian language in the first year of primary, middle and high school. 

Meloni described the measures as “common-sense tools that do not divide but really help to integrate”.

The announcement comes as Italy moves towards an expected national election in 2027, with immigration, Islam and national identity once again central battlegrounds on the political right.

Meloni’s speech and the legislation immediately raised practical questions: who exactly is “foreign” and who is Italian? 

Italy already has guidelines recommending a 30 percent ceiling for pupils without Italian citizenship. The distinction between “Italian” and “foreign” children also rests on citizenship, rather than on where children were born or have grown up. 

Italy's citizenship system is based primarily on descent: children born in the country to non-Italian parents generally do not acquire Italian citizenship automatically. 

As a result, children who were born in Italy and have spent their lives there can still be officially classified as foreign citizens. And Meloni's intervention did not come in isolation.

A mosque in Mestre

Last week, a banner declaring “Your integration is our ruin” appeared outside a school in Mestre, on the mainland opposite Venice, in an area with a large Bangladeshi community. Nearby, at a public park used by Muslims for Friday prayers, “No Islam” and Christian crosses were painted on the ground and on a wooden structure.

The incidents come as a dispute over plans by members of Mestre's Bangladeshi community to build a permanent mosque and Islamic centre on the site of a former sawmill becomes increasingly heated. The community has bought the land, but the project requires approval from local authorities.

'We cannot allow an immigrant to become an Italian citizen so easily because then this citizen votes'

- Roberto Vannacci, Futuro Nazionale

One of the project's most vocal opponents has been Anna Maria Cisint, a European parliament member for the right-wing Lega party who has repeatedly campaigned against the construction of new mosques. 

In February, during a Lega protest outside the proposed site in Mestre, Cisint declared that the mosque would not be built if her political camp remained in power.

On the same Sunday that Meloni announced her school measures, Cisint appeared at the Lega’s annual rally in Pontida, the northern Italian town that has hosted the party's symbolic gathering for decades. 

She was joined on stage by four activists from Nemesis, a French far-right group that describes itself as feminist. The activists were wearing full-face veils. As people on stage and in the crowd chanted “take it off”, the women removed them.

“The threat is radical Islam,” Cisint told the rally. “We will never allow them to Islamise our home. Never.”

The convergence was striking. In Rome, Meloni warned that Italian children could become a minority in classrooms; at Pontida, a coalition politician warned of the country’s “Islamisation”; and in Mestre, a mosque dispute was enflamed by anti-Muslim slogans.

The rogue general

At the same time, another political force is trying to carve out space further to the right.

Roberto Vannacci, a former army general who first became a national figure after publishing a book attacking immigration, feminism and LGBTQ+ rights, entered the European Parliament in 2024 with the Lega. 

The “rogue general” later broke with the party and founded Futuro Nazionale, a new far-right movement that has made “remigration” - the removal of migrants from Italy - one of its defining themes. 

The party is now registering around eight percent in some opinion polls ahead of the next general election, while the Lega, still led by Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini, has fallen below six percent. The figures have intensified a struggle over voters on the Italian right and over how far its politics on immigration and national identity can move.

It was against this backdrop that Vannacci made one of his most explicit statements yet about who should be allowed to become Italian. Speaking at a conference on urban security organised by a police union in Turin on 18 September, he argued that Italy should not make citizenship easier for immigrants.

“We cannot allow an immigrant to become an Italian citizen so easily because then this citizen votes,” Vannacci said. “And when he votes, he does not vote for the good of Italian citizens but for his own good.”

When challenged over whether he was simply worried that naturalised citizens would not vote for him, Vannacci replied: “I'm not afraid that they won't vote for me. I'm afraid that they won't vote for Italy.”

Who gets to be Italian?

The former general’s argument raises a fundamental question: what happens when the person born or raised in Italy actually becomes Italian. 

Fioralba Duma, an Italian-Albanian activist with the campaign group Italians Without Citizenship, told Middle East Eye that Meloni's remarks were particularly troubling because many of the children described as “foreign” have never known another country.

“It is sad, because you realise how little responsibility those in power take when dealing with such important issues, and how little they do to protect children and guarantee them equal opportunities,” she said.

'Petrol is approaching three euros a litre, and she is talking about girls wearing the niqab at school when there are no girls wearing the niqab at school'

- Ahmed Vall, Islamic Community of Rome

“Our struggle started 10 years ago - and for many people even earlier - but instead of reducing the number of people who are foreigners only on paper, that number continues to grow every year. We used to talk about newly arrived migrants. Today we are talking about third generations: the grandchildren of immigrants, born in Italy.”

Duma’s comments point to a contradiction that has become increasingly visible in Italy's political debate. 

Politicians can speak of “foreign pupils” in classrooms even when those pupils were born in Italy, have spent their lives in the Italian education system and may speak Italian as their first language.

Italy's citizenship law remains largely based on jus sanguinis, or citizenship by descent. A referendum in June 2025 sought to reduce from 10 to five years the period of legal residence required for non-EU adults to apply for citizenship. 

Around two-thirds of those who voted backed the proposal, but turnout was only around 30 percent, well below the 50 percent required for the result to be valid.

The Muslim threat narrative 

The controversy over the proposed mosque in Mestre shows how these arguments are playing out beyond the classroom.

Part of the city's large Bangladeshi community wants to turn the site of the former sawmill into a permanent Islamic centre capable of hosting up to 1,500 worshippers. item.title: Pakistan look forward to ‘big test’ as Thailand loom in FIFA Asean Cup opener. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Pakistan will begin their campaign in the inaugural FIFA ASEAN Cup against a vastly higher-ranked Thailand on Saturday, with head coach Nolberto Solano describing the tournament as an opportunity for his side to measure themselves against some of Asia’s stronger teams.

The Group B Division One opener will kick off at 4:00pm local time (2:00pm PST) at the Si Jalak Harupat Stadium, with Pakistan then scheduled to face the Philippines on Sept 29 and Vietnam on Oct 2.

“We want to use this opportunity to test ourselves against teams like Thailand, Philippines and Vietnam,” Solano said at the pre-match press conference on Friday. “It’s an honour to be here and we know it will be a tough competition.”

The challenge facing Pakistan is reflected in the FIFA rankings. Thailand are currently 94th, while Pakistan are 198th in the latest official rankings.

The Philippines are 135th and Vietnam 113th.

“All our opponents will be very tough and they have fantastic players,” Solano said. “Asian football has been getting better and better so it is a big test for us.

“We are slowly growing, we try to go step by step. We will try to prove ourselves as a national team and see how far we can go in this competition.”

For Pakistan, the tournament comes after an encouraging summer in which Solano’s side won the Diamond Jubilee International Football Tournament in the Maldives.

Pakistan went unbeaten in the four-team event, drawing 0-0 with Bangladesh before beating the Maldives 3-0 and Afghanistan 2-0 in the round-robin stage. They defeated Afghanistan by the same score in the final, with Shayek Dost and Harun Hamid scoring, to secure their first standalone international tournament title in decades.

The triumph also ended a long wait for Pakistan to reach and win a standalone tournament. Their previous final appearance had come at the 1962 Merdeka Cup, while their last tournament triumph before the Maldives success had been a shared title at the Asian Quadrangular Football Tournament in 1952.

The ASEAN Cup, however, presents a markedly different proposition.

Thailand have named a squad featuring veteran playmaker Chanathip Songkrasin, Japan-based midfielder Supachok Sarachat and English-born forward Jude Soonsup-Bell. German-based defender Nicholas Mickelson is also in the squad, under English coach Anthony Hudson.

Thailand’s squad also includes established domestic names such as Supachai Chaided of Buriram United and Peeradon Chamratsamee of Port FC, underlining the depth available to the side.

Pakistan, meanwhile, have assembled a 23-man squad that combines domestic players with a number of footballers based abroad. Captain Abdullah Iqbal will lead the side, while experienced forward Kaleemullah has returned to the national setup.

Defender Easah Suliman, who plays abroad, joined the squad in Bandung after his arrival was delayed by illness. Twenty-two members of the squad had assembled in Indonesia by Thursday, with Easah expected to link up on Friday.

The Pakistan side also includes teenage midfielder Abdul Samad, captain of the national Under-17 team, who recently signed a two-year contract with Azerbaijani champions Qarabag.

For captain Abdullah, the tournament represents a chance for the players to test themselves against opposition of a different calibre.

“It is a great opportunity for us to compete against teams at another level,” he said. “We will try to give our best.”

The FIFA ASEAN Cup is the first edition of a new FIFA tournament involving 14 teams — all 11 ASEAN members plus Bangladesh, Pakistan and Hong Kong China as guest participants. Division One, being staged in Indonesia, comprises eight teams divided into two groups, with the group winners advancing to the final and the runners-up playing for third place.

Pakistan are in the same group as three teams with considerably stronger recent records in Asian football. After Thailand, they face the Philippines on Sept 29 before meeting Vietnam on Oct 2, with all three group matches being played in Bandung except Pakistan’s final fixture against Vietnam, which is scheduled for Jakarta.

For Solano, the immediate objective is less about the size of the challenge and more about how his players respond to it.

“We are slowly growing,” the former Peru international said. “We try to go step by step. We will try to prove ourselves as a national team and see how far we can go in this competition.”
